topic: Day 2 · Causes of Lower GI Bleeding
speakerAffiliation: Virtual Teaching Hospital · Gastroenterology & Endoscopy Unit
speakerBio: Endoscopist with a special interest in obscure GI bleeding who teaches that the differential for rectal bleeding is a discipline of five clues — pain, timing, colour, volume, and age — not a list to be recited.
lectureHTML:
🎯 The case on the table

A 79-year-old woman, previously fit, is admitted with three episodes of painless, large-volume dark-red rectal bleeding over two hours. No abdominal pain, no weight loss, no diarrhoea. She takes amlodipine and, for a knee, occasional ibuprofen. HR 96, BP 118/70. As the blood is sent and fluids run, the registrar asks the question this whole session answers: which of the dozen causes of lower GI bleeding is this, and how do the clues tell them apart? Painless + arterial + elderly + large-volume is already whispering an answer — but the differential is a discipline, because the lesion you must never miss (cancer) and the lesion you must never over-treat (piles) can look deceptively similar at first glance.

1 · 🧠 Organising the differential by mechanism

Do not memorise a flat list — group the causes by mechanism, because mechanism predicts the clinical fingerprint (pain or not, arterial or venous, self-limiting or relentless, elderly or young).

MechanismPrototype causeSignature
Structural / vascular ruptureDiverticular bleedPainless, arterial, brisk, self-limiting
Abnormal vesselsAngiodysplasiaElderly, right colon, recurrent, often occult
IschaemiaIschaemic colitisPain then bleeding, transient, watershed
Inflammation / ulcerationIBD, infective colitisBloody diarrhoea, systemic features, young(er)
Ano-rectal / mechanicalHaemorrhoids, fissureBright red, outlet, usually minor
IatrogenicPost-polypectomy bleedDelayed, up to ~2 weeks after colonoscopy
NeoplasticColorectal cancerChronic/occult, iron-deficiency, change in bowel habit
Radiation injuryRadiation proctitisMonths–years after pelvic radiotherapy
Pain, timing, colour, volume, and age are the five clues. Ask them of every bleed and the mechanism — and the culprit — usually declares itself.

2 · 🩸 Diverticular bleeding — the commonest, and the great impostor of "benign"

Diverticular bleeding is the single most common cause of significant LGIB (broadly a third or more of cases). The mechanism is elegant and explains everything about how it behaves: as a diverticulum herniates through the muscular wall, it drags a vasa recta artery over its dome. Chronic injury thins that vessel until it ruptures — an arterial bleed into the lumen.

  • Painless — the bleed is a vascular rupture, not inflammation (contrast with diverticulitis, which hurts and rarely bleeds).
  • Arterial and brisk — can be large-volume and dramatic.
  • Usually self-limiting — around 75–80% stop spontaneously, but rebleeding occurs in a meaningful minority.
  • Right-sided diverticula bleed disproportionately — although diverticulosis is commonest in the sigmoid, right-sided diverticula have wider necks and thinner-walled vasa recta, so a notable share of diverticular bleeds arise in the right colon.
  • Risk amplified by NSAIDs, antiplatelets, and anticoagulants.
💡 One-liner

Painless, brisk, arterial rectal bleeding in an older adult that stops on its own is diverticular until proven otherwise — but "stops on its own" is not "cured": it rebleeds.

3 · 🕸️ Angiodysplasia — abnormal vessels, quiet and recurrent

Angiodysplasia (angioectasia) are dilated, thin-walled, tortuous submucosal veins and capillaries — degenerative vascular malformations, not tumours. They are a leading cause of recurrent, obscure and occult LGIB, especially in the elderly.

  • Elderly, right colon (caecum and ascending) — the classic location.
  • Recurrent and often occult — can present as iron-deficiency anaemia and intermittent bleeds rather than one dramatic event; frequently negative between episodes.
  • Associations to remember: aortic stenosis (Heyde syndrome — acquired von Willebrand type 2A from shear across the stenotic valve), chronic kidney disease, and von Willebrand disease.
  • Endoscopically: flat, red, fern-like lesions; treatable with argon plasma coagulation.
🎯 Heyde syndrome

The triad of aortic stenosis + GI angiodysplasia bleeding + acquired von Willebrand syndrome. High shear across the stenotic valve unfolds and cleaves large vWF multimers, impairing platelet plugging exactly where fragile angiodysplastic vessels leak. Definitive treatment of the bleeding can be aortic valve replacement, which reverses the vWF defect.

4 · 🚫 Ischaemic colitis — pain first, then blood

Ischaemic colitis is transient, non-occlusive hypoperfusion of the colon — the commonest form of intestinal ischaemia. The temporal signature is the teaching point: crampy abdominal pain and urgency come FIRST, then bloody, loose stool follows (usually not large-volume). It typically affects watershed zones between two arterial territories:

  • Splenic flexure (Griffiths' point) — SMA/IMA watershed.
  • Rectosigmoid junction (Sudeck's point) — IMA/superior rectal watershed.
  • The rectum is usually spared (dual blood supply including systemic).

Triggers: hypotension/shock, cardiac surgery or AAA repair, vasoconstrictors/cocaine, and it can follow a run of low flow in the elderly. Most cases are transient and resolve with supportive care; CT may show thickened, oedematous colon; colonoscopy shows segmental, sharply demarcated mucosa. Beware the minority with gangrenous/transmural ischaemia (peritonism, lactate, sepsis) who need surgery.

💡 The discriminator

Bleeding that is preceded by pain points to ischaemia; bleeding that is painless points to diverticular or angiodysplasia. Pain-then-blood in a watershed distribution is ischaemic colitis until proven otherwise.

5 · 🔥 IBD, infective and anorectal causes

Inflammatory bowel disease

Ulcerative colitis (and colonic Crohn's) cause bloody diarrhoea with mucus, urgency, tenesmus, often in a younger patient with systemic features (weight loss, raised CRP/faecal calprotectin). Acute severe UC is itself an emergency (Truelove & Witts criteria) but rarely presents as isolated massive arterial haemorrhage.

Infectious colitis

Bloody diarrhoea + fever + a food/travel history. Organisms: Campylobacter, Shigella, non-typhoidal Salmonella, enterohaemorrhagic E. coli O157 (watch for HUS — avoid antibiotics), Entamoeba histolytica, and Clostridioides difficile. Send stool cultures/PCR before reflexively scoping.

Haemorrhoids and anorectal disease

Bright red blood coating the stool, on the paper, or dripping into the pan, usually small-volume, often with straining, itch, or a lump. Fissures give bright red blood with severe defecatory pain. These are the commonest cause of minor rectal bleeding overall.

⚠️ Never attribute a major or unexplained bleed to "piles"

Haemorrhoids are so common that almost everyone has them — which makes them the most dangerous distractor in medicine. A visible pile does not exclude a synchronous colorectal cancer or angiodysplasia bleeding higher up. Attributing significant, dark, or altered blood, or bleeding with anaemia/weight loss/altered bowel habit, to haemorrhoids without imaging the colon is how curable cancers are missed. Bright-red outlet bleeding in an under-40 with an obvious fissure can be treated on its merits; anything else needs the colon visualised.

6 · 🪝 Post-polypectomy bleeding — the delayed iatrogenic bleed

After endoscopic polyp removal, bleeding can be immediate (at the procedure) or, crucially, delayed — typically 1 to 14 days later (occasionally cited up to ~2 weeks) as the diathermy eschar sloughs and exposes the vessel in the resection base.

  • Risk rises with large polyps (>2 cm), right-sided location, pedunculated polyps with a thick stalk, and resumption of antithrombotics.
  • The history makes the diagnosis: always ask about a recent colonoscopy/polypectomy in any fresh LGIB.
  • Usually endoscopically treatable (clip the visible vessel/base) — a satisfying, findable, fixable cause.

7 · 🎯 Colorectal malignancy & radiation proctitis

Colorectal cancer more often causes chronic, occult blood loss presenting as iron-deficiency anaemia, a change in bowel habit, or altered/mixed blood than a massive acute bleed — but it does bleed, and it is the diagnosis you cannot afford to miss. Red flags: age >50 (younger now rising), weight loss, tenesmus, iron-deficiency in a man or post-menopausal woman, family history. Any LGIB without a clear benign explanation warrants colonic visualisation to exclude it.

Radiation proctitis follows pelvic radiotherapy (prostate, cervical, rectal) — sometimes months to years later. Chronic telangiectasia in the rectum bleed slowly and recurrently; endoscopy shows friable mucosa with abnormal vessels, treatable with argon plasma coagulation, sucralfate enemas, or hyperbaric oxygen. The history of radiotherapy is the whole clue.

8 · 📋 Master table — cause → typical patient → clue → management

CauseTypical patientKey clueFirst-line management
DiverticularOlder, NSAID/antiplatelet userPainless, brisk, arterial, self-limiting; right colon over-representedResuscitate; colonoscopic clip/band; embolisation if ongoing
AngiodysplasiaElderly; AS, CKD, vWDRecurrent/occult, right colon, iron-deficiency; HeydeArgon plasma coagulation; treat AS if Heyde; iron
Ischaemic colitisElderly, vascular/hypotension, post-AAAPain then bleeding, watershed, transient, rectal sparingSupportive (fluids, bowel rest, antibiotics); surgery if gangrene
IBDYounger, relapsingBloody diarrhoea + mucus, systemic, ↑calprotectin/CRPTreat the IBD (steroids/biologics); scope + biopsy
Infective colitisAny; travel/food historyBloody diarrhoea + feverStool cultures/PCR; supportive; targeted antibiotics (avoid in EHEC)
Haemorrhoids / fissureAny; straining, young for fissureBright red, outlet, minor; pain with fissureConservative (fibre, topical); band/ligate — but exclude proximal cause
Post-polypectomyRecent colonoscopy (≤2 weeks)Delayed bleed after polyp removalRepeat colonoscopy + clip the base
Colorectal cancerOlder; iron-deficiency, weight lossChronic/occult, altered blood, change in habitColonoscopy + biopsy; staging; MDT/surgery
Radiation proctitisPrior pelvic radiotherapyRecurrent rectal bleed months–years laterAPC, sucralfate enema, hyperbaric O2

9 · ⚖️ Contrast pairs that trip people up

🎯 Three discriminations worth over-learning

Diverticular vs angiodysplasia: both painless and often right-sided in the elderly — but diverticular is a single brisk arterial event that stops, whereas angiodysplasia is recurrent, lower-volume, and prone to iron-deficiency. Diverticulitis vs diverticular bleeding: the -itis hurts and rarely bleeds; the bleed is painless and rarely infected — different beasts from the same anatomy. Ischaemic colitis vs infective/IBD colitis: all cause bloody loose stool, but ischaemia is pain-then-blood in a watershed segment of an older vasculopath and resolves; infection has fever and a stool-culture answer; IBD is chronic/relapsing with raised calprotectin.

☠️ M&M — the cancer that was called "haemorrhoids" for eight months

A 61-year-old man saw his GP three times over eight months with intermittent rectal bleeding. On the first visit an external haemorrhoid was noted, and each subsequent bleed was attributed to it; he was given topical treatment and reassured. No one performed a digital rectal examination beyond the first visit, and his mild microcytic anaemia (Hb 108, MCV 76, ferritin 8) was ascribed to "the piles." He finally represented with obstruction; colonoscopy revealed a near-obstructing rectosigmoid adenocarcinoma with liver metastases — now incurable. Lessons: (1) haemorrhoids are ubiquitous and a visible pile never excludes a proximal malignancy; (2) iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or post-menopausal woman is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise — it is not "from piles"; (3) altered, dark, or persistent bleeding, weight change, or altered bowel habit mandates colonic visualisation; (4) repeated identical presentations should escalate suspicion, not entrench a benign label. Anchoring on the easy diagnosis converted a curable cancer into a terminal one.

10 · 🎯 Take-home messages

  1. Group causes by mechanism — vascular rupture, abnormal vessels, ischaemia, inflammation, mechanical, iatrogenic, neoplastic, radiation — because mechanism predicts the clinical fingerprint.
  2. Diverticular bleeding is the commonest: painless, arterial (a ruptured vasa recta), brisk, usually self-limiting (~75–80%), right colon over-represented, but it rebleeds.
  3. Angiodysplasia = elderly, right colon, recurrent/occult; remember Heyde (aortic stenosis + acquired vWD).
  4. Ischaemic colitis is pain-THEN-blood in a watershed segment (splenic flexure, rectosigmoid) with rectal sparing, usually transient.
  5. Bright-red outlet bleeding is usually haemorrhoids/fissure — but never pin a major, altered, or anaemia-associated bleed on piles; exclude a proximal cancer.
  6. Ask about recent polypectomy — delayed post-polypectomy bleeding occurs up to ~2 weeks later and is usually endoscopically fixable.
  7. Iron-deficiency anaemia + rectal bleeding = image the colon — colorectal cancer is the miss you cannot afford.

moderatorQs.q: A 78-year-old presents with painless, brisk, large-volume rectal bleeding that stops on its own. What is the most likely cause, and what is the mechanism?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: This is the classic picture of diverticular bleeding — the single commonest cause of significant lower GI bleeding. The mechanism is a ruptured vasa recta artery: as a diverticulum herniates through the colonic wall it drags this penetrating vessel over its dome, where chronic injury (amplified by NSAIDs and antithrombotics) thins and ruptures it into the lumen. That arterial origin explains the brisk, large-volume nature, and the absence of inflammation explains why it is painless (unlike diverticulitis). Around 75–80% stop spontaneously, but a meaningful minority rebleed, so 'settled' is not 'cured'. Note that although diverticulosis is commonest in the sigmoid, right-sided diverticula bleed disproportionately because of their wider necks and thinner vessels.

moderatorQs.q: How do you distinguish ischaemic colitis from diverticular bleeding and from infective colitis at the bedside?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: The temporal and character clues separate them. Ischaemic colitis is pain-THEN-blood: crampy abdominal pain and urgency come first, followed by loose, bloody (usually not large-volume) stool, in an older vasculopath or after a hypotensive/low-flow insult, typically in a watershed segment (splenic flexure — Griffiths' point; rectosigmoid — Sudeck's point) with rectal sparing, and it is usually transient. Diverticular bleeding is painless, brisk, arterial, and self-limiting. Infective colitis gives bloody diarrhoea with fever and a travel/food history and is diagnosed on stool culture/PCR. So I anchor on: is there pain, and did it precede the blood (ischaemia)? Is there fever and diarrhoea (infection)? Or is it painless and brisk (diverticular)?

moderatorQs.q: A patient has an obvious bleeding haemorrhoid and iron-deficiency anaemia. Is it safe to attribute the bleeding to the pile?
moderatorQs.answerHTML: No — this combination is a red flag, not reassurance. Haemorrhoids are ubiquitous, so a visible pile never excludes a synchronous proximal lesion, and iron-deficiency anaemia in a man or post-menopausal woman is colorectal cancer until proven otherwise — haemorrhoids cause minor, bright-red outlet bleeding and are an uncommon cause of significant iron-deficiency. The mandatory step is to visualise the whole colon (colonoscopy) to exclude malignancy and angiodysplasia before ascribing anything to the pile. Treating the haemorrhoid and discharging this patient is exactly the anchoring error that turns curable cancers into terminal ones. Bright-red outlet bleeding in a young patient with an obvious fissure and normal bloods can be managed on its merits; this patient cannot.

audienceQs.q: What is Heyde syndrome and why does it matter for a colonic bleed?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Heyde syndrome is the association of aortic stenosis, bleeding GI angiodysplasia, and acquired von Willebrand syndrome (type 2A). The high shear stress as blood is forced through the stenotic valve mechanically unfolds and cleaves the large von Willebrand factor multimers that platelets need to plug small vessels — so the fragile, dilated angiodysplastic vessels in the (usually right) colon bleed and can't form a stable clot. It matters because the bleeding is often recurrent and refractory to local endoscopic treatment alone, and the definitive fix can be aortic valve replacement, which restores the vWF multimers and stops the bleeding. So in an elderly patient with recurrent angiodysplasia bleeding, listen for an ejection systolic murmur and get an echo.

audienceQs.q: A patient bleeds 10 days after a colonoscopy with polypectomy. Is that related, and does it change what drugs I flag?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Yes, almost certainly related — this is classic delayed post-polypectomy bleeding, which typically occurs anywhere from about 1 to 14 days after the procedure as the diathermy eschar sloughs and exposes the vessel in the resection base. Risk is higher with large (>2 cm) or right-sided polyps and, importantly for you, with resumption of antithrombotics — so I'd flag exactly when and which antiplatelet/anticoagulant was restarted, whether the timing matched guideline advice, and whether it needs holding again around a repeat scope. The good news is it's usually endoscopically treatable — the endoscopist clips the visible vessel — so the priority is a prompt repeat colonoscopy plus a sensible antithrombotic plan, balanced against the reason they were anticoagulated.

audienceQs.q: Young patient, massive painless lower GI bleed, colonoscopy and gastroscopy both normal. What am I missing?
audienceQs.answerHTML: Think small-bowel source beyond the reach of both scopes — in a young adult with a painless massive bleed the classic culprit is a Meckel's diverticulum containing ectopic gastric mucosa, which secretes acid and ulcerates the adjacent ileum. A Meckel's (technetium-99m pertechnetate) scan can identify the ectopic gastric mucosa. Other small-bowel causes include angiodysplasia/Dieulafoy lesions and, rarely, small-bowel tumours; the work-up if the Meckel's scan is negative is CT angiography (if actively bleeding) and capsule endoscopy or device-assisted enteroscopy when settled. The key mental shift is that a normal colonoscopy plus gastroscopy does not exclude GI bleeding — it just moves the search to the segment neither scope reaches.
